issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
issues.explanation: Within-node contradiction: endorsing both undereating/restricting food and overeating as coping strategies is hard to reconcile as simultaneous characteristic strategies without further qualification; these items express opposing behavioral patterns within the same node.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Overeating: I eat more than usual to distract myself or feel better
issues.explanation: Cross-node/formulation mismatch: door and lock checking implies a home-intrusion or direct personal safety threat focus, but the trauma type is trauma to a loved one and the rest of the profile centers on intrusive memory, guilt, startle, and false alarms rather than a coherent intrusion-specific threat theme. This item feels weakly integrated with the other selected items.

issues.item: Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: Cross-node mismatch: intense guilt on recall is typically more naturally linked to negative appraisals, yet no negative appraisal content is endorsed and that node is formulation-inactive. On its own this is not impossible, but here it sits somewhat incoherently beside a profile otherwise dominated by perceptual re-experiencing and generalized danger responses.

issues.item: Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
issues.explanation: This item is internally contradictory as written: 'Avoid Thinking' implies cognitive avoidance, but the selected statement 'Thinking about the event' expresses the opposite state. Within-node inconsistency is clear enough to question whether this item was selected correctly. The rest of the profile is clinically coherent for trauma to a loved one with strong Memory–Threat–Maladaptive Strategy links.

issues.item: Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, these threat/strategy items imply a current fear of direct interpersonal or home-intrusion danger to self. That can occur, but here it is hard to reconcile clinically with the rest of the profile, which is centered on guilt-laden, fragmented, sensory memories of the loved one’s trauma rather than a personally attacked or pursued threat context.

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: The strong formulation links are Memory ↔ Threat and Threat → Maladaptive Strategies. The selected memory items plausibly drive guilt and sensory re-experiencing, but they do not support a specific pattern of being watchful for dangerous people and compulsively checking locks. Those items look tailored to ongoing personal danger and are not well explained by the reported trauma type or by the rest of the node content.

The profile is broadly severe and internally linked, but one memory item is hard to reconcile with the trauma type and the rest of the formulation: for trauma to a loved one, intense guilt on recall is possible, yet here there are no corresponding negative appraisal items about responsibility, failure, or preventability, making this guilt-specific memory stand out as clinically under-supported.

Threat items emphasize immediate personal danger and home-intrusion style fear (startling to nearby movement, repeated door/window checking), which fits direct interpersonal threat more than trauma to a loved one unless the loved one’s trauma also left the patient fearing attack. That extension is not supported elsewhere in the selected items.

Hypervigilance towards dangerous people coheres with the same personal-danger theme, but that theme is not grounded by the trauma type or by memory content, which centers guilt, fragmentation, and auditory recall rather than being targeted at dangerous people. This creates a cross-node mismatch.

vignette:
Kiet Tran was sixty-eight years old, a public defender for over three decades, when his wife Linh was killed in their home. He had been late that night, working on a brief for a client charged with armed robbery. The office had been tense; the prosecution had filed a last-minute motion, and Kiet had stayed until nearly eleven. When he got home, the front door was ajar. He still could not hold the next few minutes together in his mind. There were pieces: the hallway light flickering, the overturned plant stand, the sound of his own breathing. He remembered kneeling-or maybe he had fallen-and then the paramedics were there, and someone was asking him if he could hear them. But the memory that came most often, unbidden, was not a picture but a sound: a single, muffled thud that he had taken for the front door closing, only to realise later it must have been something else. That sound played in his head when he least expected it, during a quiet moment in court or while he was pouring his morning coffee. What came with it was a grief so sudden and complete that he would have to grip the edge of the sink or the arm of his chair.

In the months after Linh's death, Kiet began to notice changes in himself that he at first attributed to ordinary mourning. He started checking the locks on his apartment door twice, then three times, then four before he could settle into sleep. He would get up in the middle of the night to check again, even though he knew he had locked it. He began scanning the faces of people in the grocery store, in the courthouse hallway, on the sidewalk-searching for someone who looked like a threat. He had always been alert in his work, but now it was different. He was certain that dangerous people were everywhere, that any man in a hoodie or a cap pulled low could be the one. At work, he found himself avoiding new clients who reminded him of the man whose case had kept him late that night. He stopped watching crime dramas or reading the news about home invasions. When a colleague recommended a documentary about wrongful convictions, Kiet muttered that he did not have the time. The truth was that the preview alone had made his hands shake.

His eating changed. He would come home from work and sit in front of the television, not watching anything in particular, and eat whatever was easiest-chips, leftover takeout, whole sleeves of crackers-not because he was hungry but because the chewing and swallowing filled something. He gained weight, which his doctor mentioned at a check-up, but Kiet could not bring himself to care. The false alarms, as he thought of them, wore him down most. A car backfiring in the parking lot would send his heart racing. A sudden knock at the door would leave him frozen, his breath shallow, until he peered through the peephole and saw only a neighbour collecting a package. Each time, the rush of fear was followed by a wave of shame. He was a grown man, a public defender who had faced angry defendants and hostile judges; why was he cowering in his own hallway? And then came the guilt-heavy and sticky-for having been late, for having been so absorbed in a stranger's case that he had not been home. He told himself it was irrational, but the feeling did not go away.

His memories of that night remained splintered. He could not reconstruct the sequence. He knew he had called 911, but he could not hear his own voice. He knew he had held Linh's hand, but he could not feel it. Only the sound-that thud-was sharp and clear. Whenever the fragments surfaced, usually late at night or during a slow moment in the office, he was overtaken by a grief that felt as fresh as the first day. He had not cried in years before then; now he sometimes found tears streaming down his face without warning.

What finally brought him to a clinic was an incident in the courthouse elevator. A young man in a hoodie stepped in beside him, and Kiet's breath caught. He pressed himself into the corner, his heart slamming, and when the doors opened he all but ran out. He stood in the lobby, trembling, and realised that he could not go on this way. He called a number he had clipped from an advertisement weeks earlier. He did not know if talking would help, but he was tired of checking locks, of flinching at sounds, of being afraid in a world that had already taken everything. He hoped that somewhere, someone might help him piece the fragments back together, or at least teach him how to live with what they left behind.
